title: HIDA after equivocal gallbladder ultrasound

cues.phrase: The common duct is not dilated; bilirubin is within the laboratory reference range.
cues.why: Weakens the duct-imaging alternative, but does not distinguish the two scintigraphy protocols without clinical knowledge. Necessary localization, not a sufficient shortcut.

fairness: Exact five visible fields and version match the pre-round-four snapshot. Inflammatory findings versus ultrasound components, then filling versus emptying protocols, still support one best offered answer.

Scope of this report: 73 versions (43 main plus 30 context questions). Judgments use only the current after Presentation, Current update, Exhibit, Task and Options. Prior responses, explanations and future results are not evidence of quality. Difficulty is an uncalibrated PGY-2/3 prediction; PASS is editorial, not clinical approval.

All 27 retained PASS versions and three accepted-basic versions match the saved pre-round-four packet; B01/B10 overlap those groups. The eleven separate owner-approved versions also match baseline live presentation, complaint, profiles, question version, task, update, exhibit and choice fields. They are outside these two packets and are not added to the 73-item denominator.

No network was used. Local source ledgers were checked for claim mappings and exact-value provenance; their accounts of external verification were not independently authenticated. No new exact clinical cutoff is proposed.
suggestions: Retain the necessary observations and close protocol alternatives.

title: Classify nipple discharge patterns

suggestions: Retain; the medication name and raw discharge observations are decision-relevant rather than answer labels.

title: Select diagnostic imaging for pathologic discharge

title: Perioperative ART continuity
fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. The named ART combination must be interpreted before choosing both continuity and midazolam route. Oral midazolam is a proposed plan to evaluate, not a reason to select it. The crossed choices remain fair.

title: Apply benzodiazepine-antagonist contraindication after seizure control
fairness: The convulsions without recovery identify a serious seizure-control indication, while shallow breathing creates a credible reason to consider reversal. The learner must distinguish reversal of sedation from antagonizing treatment of that seizure state. Supported ventilation makes withholding the antagonist an actionable instruction rather than ignoring respiratory depression.

Withhold versus give-now/give-after-another-drug is an intentional timing decision; the short negative key has no unique explanatory padding. The local claim claim.qq20261102c.flumazenil-seizure-control-contraindication maps this boundary to the DailyMed label. This offline review does not independently verify the label.
The task is specifically the reversal instruction. It would be incomplete as a comprehensive seizure/airway management plan, but does not purport to be one.
suggestions: Retain for anesthesia/neurology confirmation of the exact scenario. Keep assisted ventilation and the seizure course; neither is a dispensable cue.

title: Manometric recognition of achalasia
fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. This is straightforward pressure-pattern recognition, with one defensible offered diagnosis. Ease is acceptable only for the already accepted foundational role, not as a resident challenge.
suggestions: Retain the accepted basic designation.

title: Resolve technical and symptom-protocol limitations in motility testing

cues.phrase: No endoscopically assisted placement was attempted.
cues.why: Names the untried maneuver that appears only in the key, allowing a missing-step matching strategy without interpreting the pressure recording.

cues.phrase: Manometry with endoscopic catheter placement
cues.why: Repeats the specifically highlighted missing maneuver. Unlike the other choices, it lacks an initial 'Obtain'; this is a small grammar outlier, not the main defect.

fairness: Failure to cross the junction followed by an assisted attempt is a defensible pathway; FLIP is a real complementary alternative rather than an absurd distractor. The meaningful reasoning is recognizing an uninterpretable junction acquisition and selecting how to complete it.

The current cue weakens that reasoning. The local ledger describes assisted completion as a case-specific application, not proof that every failed study must be repeated before FLIP. The comparison needs specialist confirmation, particularly when retching/tolerance is the obstacle.
suggestions: Delete the sentence naming unattempted endoscopic assistance; the blind-advancement record already describes what was tried. Preserve the catheter position and reason the test stopped.

Use parallel procedure labels. Ask the clinician to confirm that assisted completion is preferred for this particular failed attempt; if tolerance makes FLIP equally appropriate, change the clinical circumstances or option set rather than declare FLIP universally inferior.

title: Manometric recognition of achalasia
fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. Position-dependent relaxation measurements compete with absent contractility in every swallow. This requires classification and the resulting corroboration/treatment decision, rather than matching a diagnosis label.
The exact DCI/protocol values are retained, not newly introduced this round. Clinical classification confirmation remains separate from this editorial retention.
suggestions: Retain the primary/secondary-position distinction and close outflow-obstruction alternative.

title: Resolve technical and symptom-protocol limitations in motility testing

cues.phrase: no spaced-swallow series or alternate-position series is saved.
cues.why: Explicitly advertises an incomplete protocol; only the key completes testing, while both distractors commit to treatment from that incomplete assessment.

cues.phrase: Repeat a complete high-resolution manometry study
cues.why: The reassuring word 'complete' directly repairs the announced absence. A test-wise reader can choose it without knowing deglutitive inhibition.

fairness: The saved swallowing sequence does not justify either offered treatment classification, so repeat adequate testing is defensible. The problem is difficulty, not a confident clinical error.

Too easy for the stated resident goal: the diagnostic-workup-versus-premature-treatment contrast removes the need to understand why overlapping swallows distort the tracing. The current two-step claim is not earned.
suggestions: Keep the actual acquisition sequence but compare plausible ways of resolving it at the same decision stage, such as appropriately specified repeat acquisition versus a clinically credible complementary study.

Have the distinguishing choice depend on interpretation of rapid-swallow inhibition, not on choosing the only option that obtains missing data. Do not remove the acquisition information needed for fairness.

title: Manometric recognition of achalasia

cues.phrase: The prescribing team can supervise a medication adjustment, and the patient can maintain oral intake during reassessment.
cues.why: Favors the reassessment axis, but applies to two alternatives and supplies genuine feasibility/safety context. It cannot choose the motility interpretation by itself.

fairness: The elevated junction relaxation measure and premature contractions must be distinguished from distal spasm, then interpreted in light of oxycodone exposure before irreversible treatment planning. Withdrawal/reassessment and pattern classification are both needed.

No arbitrary washout period or dose was added. 'Coordinated opioid withdrawal' should remain a supervised plan rather than imply abrupt discontinuation. The current update resolves the earlier inability-to-reassess problem.
suggestions: Retain the dual-axis choices and supervised feasibility information; specialist review should confirm the medication-associated classification language.

title: Resolve technical and symptom-protocol limitations in motility testing

cues.phrase: none of the water swallows reproduces it.
cues.why: Pairs the symptom-trigger mismatch with an option that simply supplies food instead of water.

cues.phrase: The study has no meal or provocative-swallow recording.
cues.why: Names the missing test-meal component that only the key offers.

cues.phrase: High-resolution manometry with another water-swallow series
cues.why: 'Another' repeats the explicitly unsuccessful provocation, making the closest-looking alternative self-defeating.

fairness: Provocative meal assessment is a defensible offered next test for the supplied symptom discrepancy. Structural and eosinophilic exclusion are useful clinical background.
Too easy for residents as written: food causes symptoms, water does not, and the key is the only food-based investigation. This is a direct repair rule rather than two substantive inferences.
suggestions: Remove the sentence naming the absent meal recording and the dismissive 'another' option wording.

Rebuild the comparison around credible investigations for persistent solid-food dysphagia, with enough actual findings to distinguish a provocative motility study from a supported alternative. Obtain source support before adding protocol details.

title: Manometric recognition of achalasia
fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. Marked resistance and weight loss still require investigation for secondary junction disease despite achalasia-like physiology. The raw DCI range and trace description support the physiology interpretation.
Both pattern classification and the secondary-lesion assessment must be correct; the crossed choices remain fair. No new clinical or presentation defect was identified in the retained version.
suggestions: Retain the measured pressure findings, weight trajectory and actual endoscopic resistance rather than an interpreted secondary-disease label.

title: Resolve technical and symptom-protocol limitations in motility testing
fairness: The report's numerical conclusion competes with raw evidence of catheter displacement and absent gastric baseline. Recognizing that the junction value is not trustworthy, then choosing an assisted pressure acquisition rather than merely accepting the report, requires technical knowledge.

The named tests are necessary alternatives. Neither 'endoscopic catheter placement' nor its rationale is explicitly supplied by the stem. FLIP is clinically plausible, but the record describes one failed outside acquisition rather than unsuccessful assisted completion; the keyed next attempt is defensible among these choices.
Local claim claim.qq20261102c.hrm-incomplete-placement supports the acquisition limitation, with case-specific ranking still requiring motility review.
suggestions: Retain, with clinician confirmation of assisted manometry versus FLIP for this acquisition failure. Align option grammar without adding rationales.

title: Resolve occult-groin imaging and symptom discordance

cues.phrase: The outside ultrasound was obtained supine at rest with the probe over the painful hip-flexor origin.
cues.why: Contrasts an at-rest, differently located scan with a swelling triggered by lifting. A reader can infer the test never examined the problem without medical knowledge.

cues.phrase: The saved images do not include coughing or straining.
cues.why: Announces the missing dynamic component; only the key supplies it.

cues.phrase: Hernia unresolved; dynamic groin ultrasound
cues.why: Only this option permits uncertainty after an obviously incomplete examination; both distractors make definitive opposite diagnoses.

fairness: Repeating a targeted dynamic examination is defensible. The report's negative result does not establish exclusion, and a photograph alone need not establish a repair indication.
Too easy for residents: the alternatives are overconfident diagnoses versus a plainly incomplete test. No second clinical inference is required.
suggestions: Keep sufficient acquisition facts to establish the limitation, but remove the redundant omission sentence.

Use a credible competing next investigation or a genuinely plausible alternate pain-management plan rather than both 'excluded' and 'established' extremes. Supply a source-supported discriminator if ranking ultrasound against MRI.

title: Apply symptom attribution to a demonstrated inguinal hernia

cues.phrase: Hip rotation reproduces a separate deep ache.
cues.why: Explicitly partitions two problems; the key is the only option that deals with both without dismissing either.

cues.phrase: Discuss elective hernia repair without hip assessment
cues.why: The 'without' clause advertises neglect of the second documented complaint.

cues.phrase: Discuss hernia repair and hip-pain assessment
cues.why: Combines the useful component of each distractor, a classic convergence/completeness shortcut.

fairness: A repair discussion plus evaluation of the other pain source is reasonable. A minimally symptomatic reducible hernia in a man can also be observed; the stem does not quantify burden or patient goals enough to portray observation as categorically wrong.
Too easy as a 'remember both complaints' item, and the broad discussion key is more inclusive than the alternatives.
suggestions: Replace the 'without hip assessment' distractor with a realistic management sequence that does not announce an omission.

Specify the actual clinical decision and meaningful symptom burden/goals, then compare equally comprehensive plans. Do not invent a preference solely to force surgery or promise that repair cures the deep pain.

title: Resolve occult-groin imaging and symptom discordance

cues.phrase: An experienced examiner
cues.why: An author-supplied quality endorsement weakens the repeat-ultrasound choice before the reader evaluates the actual saved views. The acquisition details already establish what was tested.

fairness: Adequate dynamic ultrasound with the actual symptoms reproduced is a meaningful change from an incomplete study. MRI can investigate occult hernia and musculoskeletal pathology.

The competing sports-medicine assessment with reassessment is also defensible: the described limiting pain is reproduced at a tender adductor attachment, and no hernia appeared during the recorded contour change. The stem lacks a reason that advanced imaging must precede a conservative musculoskeletal assessment. A general recommendation that MRI can follow negative ultrasound does not uniquely rank these choices.
This is meaningful two-step reasoning, but unresolved ranking is not legitimate difficulty.
suggestions: Remove 'An experienced examiner' and retain the actual examination conditions.

Clarify the remaining diagnostic concern and why it changes the next action despite the adequate scan, or compare imaging strategies under an explicit already-made decision to obtain further imaging. Alternatively accept the conservative assessment pathway if that fits the intended case; do not invent failed treatment or preferences without support.

title: Apply symptom attribution to a demonstrated inguinal hernia

cues.phrase: the protrusion is not tender and straining does not reproduce the limiting pain; resisted adduction reproduces the usual medial thigh pain.
cues.why: The negative/positive pairing labels one lesion as painless and the other as the exact pain source. The options then restate 'Muscle pain', 'Hernia pain' and 'Combined pain'.

fairness: Observation of a painless reducible hernia in this man while treating the musculoskeletal complaint is defensible. The record does not prove that a provocation test uniquely establishes every source of pain, but the task asks for the best initial plan rather than certainty.
Too easy for the resident target: the binary symptom attribution is supplied almost verbatim and no competing evidence has to be weighed.
suggestions: Keep necessary symptom localization but remove redundant reassurance and diagnosis-to-plan labels that simply echo it.

Test a genuinely competing attribution or management-sequencing decision using supported observations. If retaining this exact straightforward case, seek explicit acceptance of an easy role rather than resurrecting the rejected basic designation.

title: Resolve occult-groin imaging and symptom discordance

cues.phrase: the operator examined a site lateral to the photographed lump.
cues.why: An explicit wrong-site test invites 'test the correct site' without clinical reasoning.

cues.phrase: The report's skin marker and the patient's photograph place the two sites on opposite sides of the inguinal crease.
cues.why: Repeats the same mismatch, making 'unresolved' the only sensible diagnosis-certainty choice.

cues.phrase: Hernia excluded; hip-directed rehabilitation
cues.why: The alternative declares exclusion from a test that visibly missed the site; hip rehabilitation is also less grounded here than in B05, with no hip-motion findings.

fairness: Targeted repeat ultrasound is reasonable after a wrong-site examination, but the two definitive alternatives are not close resident errors under these explicit conditions.

Too easy; location matching is the whole decision. The directions 'lateral' and 'opposite sides of the inguinal crease' should also be checked for coherent anatomy rather than used as a vague marker of error.
suggestions: Use one clear, anatomically interpretable localization observation rather than two statements of wrong-site acquisition.
Offer realistic competing next steps and an observation that clinically distinguishes them. Avoid importing the hip-rehabilitation alternative unchanged from a different vignette.

title: Apply symptom attribution to a demonstrated inguinal hernia

cues.phrase: A different tender point at the adductor origin produces discomfort only with resisted hip adduction.
cues.why: Separately labels the second complaint, making the combined answer obvious.

cues.phrase: Discuss elective hernia repair without hip assessment
cues.why: States an intentional omission of an explicitly documented problem.

cues.phrase: Discuss hernia repair and hip-pain assessment
cues.why: Converges the repair and musculoskeletal-assessment components while the alternatives each neglect one.

fairness: Repair discussion and separate musculoskeletal assessment are reasonable, but observation with conservative treatment can remain a reasonable patient-centered initial plan when symptom severity and goals are unspecified.
The task's broad 'discussion' wording gives the key an inclusiveness advantage over a specific trial. This does not establish resident-level difficulty.
suggestions: Compare plans at the same scope and remove the 'without' omission.

Use the clinical burden and intended decision to distinguish repair discussion from watchful waiting, without adding an artificial preference to select the key. Do not conflate pain near the adductor origin with a proven hip-joint diagnosis.

title: Resolve occult-groin imaging and symptom discordance

cues.phrase: Two independently reviewed dynamic groin ultrasound examinations
cues.why: Discourages repeating the same examination, but the accompanying coverage/provocation findings justify this. It does not itself decide MRI versus exploration.

fairness: Interpreting adequately negative provoked studies in the setting of persistent contour symptoms and musculoskeletal provocation, then selecting cross-sectional problem solving before invasive exploration, supports a defensible best answer.

No key-only rationale, length outlier or certainty label. Dynamic MRI is a next investigation here, not a claim that every negative ultrasound mandates MRI. The clinical ranking remains subject to groin-specialist review.
suggestions: Retain the actual scan coverage and symptom reproduction. The independent-review endorsement can be shortened if the same acquisition facts are preserved.

title: Apply symptom attribution to a demonstrated inguinal hernia

cues.phrase: The visible protrusion causes no discomfort with strain; resisted trunk flexion reproduces the limiting suprapubic pain.
cues.why: Directly assigns pain away from the hernia and toward the attachment; the options simply attach management to those same labels.

fairness: The keyed conservative initial approach is defensible for a painless reducible inguinal finding in this man. The study and symptom mapping do not justify repair as treatment for the explicitly separate limiting pain.
Too easy for residents despite several observations: the deciding interpretation is effectively provided. This is not a new clinical inaccuracy.
suggestions: Replace the label-and-plan alternatives with realistic competing initial plans at the same scope.

Require weighing a meaningful competing observation or a consequential sequencing decision; do not remove the necessary symptom facts merely to create ambiguity. No automatic basic exception is accepted.

title: Resolve cystic thyroid-node imaging/cytology discordance

cues.phrase: the saved needle image shows no pass through the solid rim.
cues.why: Explicitly tells the reader the target was missed, while only the key obtains a new specimen.

cues.phrase: The outside neck ultrasound includes central and lateral compartments.
cues.why: Together with the detailed node description, it preemptively eliminates the repeat-whole-neck-ultrasound option.

cues.phrase: Repeat node FNA with cytology and thyroglobulin washout
cues.why: The key is the only targeted diagnostic completion; the alternative FNA wording defers sampling behind a scan already described as complete.

fairness: Cystic-fluid sampling does not resolve the suspicious solid-rim findings, so the keyed repeat targeted assessment is defensible. Thyroglobulin washout has interpretation limitations with an intact thyroid; its presence should not be taught as independently diagnostic.

The 12-mm observation is mapped in claim.qq20261102c.thyroid-cystic-node-discordance, not an invented new threshold. The actual offered key does not explicitly say to sample the solid rim, which is the crucial technical correction.
Too easy: both competing paths accept or repeat an obviously inadequate step instead of offering a credible alternative way to resolve the suspicious node.
suggestions: Make the key explicitly target the solid component, not merely repeat an unspecified FNA.

Compare credible specimen or staging plans with parallel specificity, and retain enough imaging/cytology information to distinguish them. Avoid adding more option-specific negatives as the sole source of difficulty.

title: Escalate complicated stoma prolapse

cues.why: Weakens the manual-reduction/outpatient path, but is an essential danger finding in the accepted safety-recognition task.

fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. Obstructive symptoms with a nonreducible swollen prolapse support escalation over outpatient review. Intentionally easy safety recognition remains fair; do not market it as difficult resident reasoning.
suggestions: Retain the accepted basic/safety role and the red flags.

title: Sentinel-node staging discussion for melanoma
fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. The depth supports considering sentinel staging despite benign-appearing basin imaging, and planned reconstruction makes timing consequential. No new fairness defect found.

title: Resolve partial skin-biopsy and microstaging limitations

cues.phrase: The report does not give a reliable maximum invasive thickness.
cues.why: Supplies the interpretation that the diagnostic workup is inadequate; only the key completes diagnosis before staging.

cues.phrase: the surrounding lax skin can be brought together around the entire lesion without tension.
cues.why: Preselects feasibility of complete removal; this is legitimate clinical information but reinforces the only diagnosis-first choice.

cues.phrase: using the current specimen report
cues.why: Both distractors explicitly depend on a report the stem has already called unreliable.

fairness: A sample from the flat edge cannot establish what remains in the raised focus. Completion before definitive staging is a defensible key. The phrase 'atypical melanocytes along the epidermal junction and reaches the deep specimen edge' needs pathology review: what tissue/process reaches the deep edge is unclear, and junctional atypia alone is not a measured invasive melanoma.
Too easy through explicit unreliability plus two alternatives knowingly using that unreliable report. The second inference is supplied.
suggestions: Describe the actual specimen depth, sampled site and retained raised focus; remove the interpretive 'reliable maximum' sentence if those observations establish the limitation.

Offer a credible targeted diagnostic alternative rather than two plans explicitly using a discredited report. Have the pathologist clarify whether the specimen is tangentially truncated epidermis, invasive tumor at the base, or only an unsampled-component problem.

title: Apply regional-node evidence before sentinel staging

cues.phrase: Distant staging has not yet been completed.
cues.why: Signals missing work that is repeated in the key, but both the key and dissection alternative include distant staging. Medical knowledge is still needed to choose its sequence and reject sentinel staging of an already proven-positive node.

fairness: Malignant melanocytes from the suspicious regional node distinguish proven regional disease from occult-node staging. The decision then concerns staging and multidisciplinary planning before committing to dissection. That is a defensible best offered pathway.
The 1.5-mm primary thickness is a constructed observation, not a new treatment cutoff. The option does not commit to a specific systemic regimen or automatically mandate node dissection.
suggestions: Retain the proven node result and sequencing alternatives. The final sentence can be shortened to an objective record of available staging studies without changing what is known.

title: Resolve partial skin-biopsy and microstaging limitations

cues.phrase: The changing asymmetric center remains, with a different surface pattern from the sampled area.
cues.why: Clearly announces that the benign fragment did not represent the target; the answer becomes 'sample what remains'.

cues.phrase: the surrounding lax skin can be brought together around the entire lesion without tension.
cues.why: Makes complete excision uniquely convenient, reducing the repeat-punch alternative to an obvious partial-sampling compromise.

fairness: Complete diagnostic excision is defensible for an accessible suspicious residual lesion. A correctly targeted punch is not inherently invalid, but the visible closure feasibility favors completion here.

Too easy for the intended resident application: changing, unsampled center versus peripheral nevus is direct sampling-adequacy recognition. The clinician/pathologist review sentence does not add their actual conclusion and cannot serve as evidence of concordance.
suggestions: Remove the bare clinician/pathologist-meeting sentence unless it supplies a decision-relevant observation.

Make the closest diagnostic alternative credible and require an actual sampling/planning distinction, or explicitly seek acceptance of an easier role. Preserve sufficient anatomy and lesion extent to justify complete versus partial sampling.

title: Oncologic regional resection for colon cancer
fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. Raw lymphovascular invasion must be recognized and translated into regional resection despite a scar and negative radiologic nodal staging. The local-excision and surveillance alternatives remain distinguishable.

fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. Poor differentiation must be inferred from the gland-poor malignant architecture, then used to select regional surgery rather than local scar treatment despite negative imaging. No new fairness concern.

fairness: The whole-body staging coverage is already adequate, but the small single-phase liver finding remains uncharacterized. Local claim claim.qq20261102c.colon-indeterminate-liver-mri expressly maps the subcentimeter scenario to ACR criteria. The 8-mm focus is a fictional observation, not a new follow-up threshold. Kidney function supplies eligibility rather than naming the chosen modality.

MRI is a defensible best offered investigation; the item does not claim that all PET or liver biopsy is inappropriate. One-source provenance and exact radiologic ranking still need clinician confirmation.

title: Oncologic regional resection for colon cancer
fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. Deep-margin involvement and unmeasurable invasion depth must be integrated rather than allowing the negative sampled lymphovascular finding or CT to clear the lesion. The surgical-fitness statement supports the offered broad management choice.

Use a clinically credible coverage/protocol alternative whose adequacy must be interpreted, or redesign around a genuine finding that changes the next investigation. Do not add an unsupported nodule-size cutoff.

title: Oncologic regional resection for colon cancer
fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. Fragmentation plus tumor within an endothelial-lined channel creates risk not resolved by a normal staging scan. The best offered broad plan remains regional colectomy.
suggestions: Retain the histologic findings; the scar is not evidence that regional treatment is unnecessary.

title: Preoperative cross-sectional staging for colon cancer
fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. A negative FDG study and localization-only CT must be distinguished from complete diagnostic staging. Repeated modality names are essential to the actual protocol comparison and do not uniquely identify the key.

fairness: Exact visible fields/version unchanged. Sentinel staging despite benign-appearing nodes and its timing relative to reconstruction remain the two decisions. No new defect found in the retained version.

title: Apply regional-node evidence before sentinel staging

The distinction between sampling a suspicious known node and looking for occult basin disease is a real resident error, so two-step reasoning remains despite the conspicuous sampling defect. A repeat targeted FNA could also be reasonable in practice, but it is not an offered competing answer.

Make the decision depend on which missing anatomical relationship changes biopsy planning, with adequate data to rank the alternatives. Do not simply pad the existing omission list.
